presentingComplaint: Recurrent episodes of severe right-upper-quadrant pain after meals, the latest lasting about 4 hours before settling.
history: Type 2 diabetic for 14 years and CKD stage 3b (baseline creatinine ~1.9 mg/dL), on metformin, gliclazide, ramipril and atorvastatin. Over the last 3 months she has had 4-5 episodes of cramping/boring right-upper-quadrant and epigastric pain, typically 30-60 minutes after a fatty meal, radiating to the right scapula, associated with nausea and occasional vomiting. Each episode builds to a plateau and self-resolves within 1-5 hours, leaving her completely well between attacks. No fever, rigors, dark urine, pale stool or itch. This presentation is a typical, more prolonged attack that had already begun to ease on arrival. Her diabetes and CKD have muddied prior assessments: an earlier ED visit attributed the pain to 'gastritis' and a raised creatinine to her known CKD, and her autonomic neuropathy blunts the intensity she reports. No prior abdominal surgery; overweight, multiparous, non-smoker, minimal alcohol.
examination: Comfortable and pain-free at the time of review, afebrile, not jaundiced. Soft abdomen with mild residual right-upper-quadrant tenderness but no guarding, no rebound and a negative Murphy sign. No palpable mass or organomegaly, bowel sounds normal. No stigmata of chronic liver disease. Mild bilateral pedal pitting oedema consistent with known CKD.

labs.creatinine: 1.9 mg/dL (at baseline for known CKD stage 3b)

imaging: Transabdominal ultrasound: multiple mobile echogenic gallstones in the gallbladder with posterior acoustic shadowing; gallbladder wall thickness normal (2 mm), no pericholecystic fluid, no sonographic Murphy sign. Common bile duct not dilated (4 mm). Liver normal echotexture; kidneys show bilateral cortical thinning consistent with chronic disease.
microbiology: Not applicable - no infective focus; blood cultures not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute cholecystitis (excluded: afebrile, normal WBC/CRP, negative sonographic Murphy, normal gallbladder wall)
Acute cholangitis (excluded: no fever, no jaundice, normal LFTs, non-dilated CBD)
Peptic ulcer disease / dyspepsia (prior mislabel; pain is clearly meal-triggered, colicky and stone-associated)
Renal colic (CKD confounder; but pain is RUQ, radiates to scapula, US shows stones in gallbladder not tract obstruction)
finalDiagnosis: Symptomatic cholelithiasis (biliary colic) in a patient with type 2 diabetes and CKD stage 3b
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Diseases of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts
American College of Gastroenterology - Clinical Guideline: Gallstone Disease, 2024
SAGES - Guidelines for the Clinical Application of Laparoscopic Biliary Tract Surgery, 2010
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis. No antibiotics are indicated for uncomplicated biliary colic; antimicrobials would represent inappropriate use. Management is analgesia (NSAIDs are relatively contraindicated given CKD stage 3b - use with caution or prefer an antispasmodic/opioid-sparing approach with careful renal dosing), antiemetics, dietary fat reduction, and referral for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy as definitive therapy. The role of the clinician here is to actively exclude cholecystitis/cholangitis/pancreatitis (which WOULD warrant antibiotics) rather than to treat the colic itself.
contraindications: NSAIDs relatively contraindicated / require caution in CKD stage 3b (nephrotoxicity, hyperkalaemia risk with concurrent ACE inhibitor)
Metformin should be reviewed/withheld peri-operatively and if eGFR falls further or with contrast imaging
Avoid nephrotoxic imaging contrast where possible given reduced eGFR
edgeCases: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can blunt pain perception, causing underestimation of biliary disease severity and delayed diagnosis
A chronically raised creatinine from CKD can wrongly anchor clinicians to a renal cause and away from the gallbladder

Diabetics are at higher risk of progressing silently to acute (including acalculous/emphysematous) cholecystitis - a change to persistent pain, fever or a positive Murphy must trigger reassessment for an infective complication
expectedMaiK: Recurrent, self-limiting, fatty-meal-triggered RUQ pain radiating to the scapula, with gallstones on ultrasound but NO fever, normal inflammatory markers, negative Murphy, normal gallbladder wall and normal LFTs/lipase, is biliary colic - not cholecystitis, cholangitis or pancreatitis. The diabetes and CKD are confounders, not the cause.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the pain episodic and self-limiting (colic) or now constant and progressive (suggesting cholecystitis)?
Any fever, rigors, jaundice, dark urine or pale stools pointing to ductal obstruction/cholangitis?
Relationship of pain to fatty meals and duration of each episode?
What is the patient's baseline creatinine/eGFR, and which nephrotoxic or renally-cleared drugs is she taking?
expectedInvestigations: Transabdominal ultrasound of the biliary tree
LFTs including bilirubin, ALP, GGT and transaminases
FBC and CRP to exclude infective/inflammatory cholecystitis
Renal function (creatinine/eGFR) against baseline before analgesia/imaging decisions

investigations: Transabdominal ultrasound of the biliary tree

regressionAssertions: Must diagnose biliary_colic (symptomatic cholelithiasis), NOT cholecystitis or cholangitis, given afebrile state, normal WBC/CRP, negative Murphy, normal gallbladder wall and normal LFTs.
Must NOT recommend antibiotics for uncomplicated biliary colic (stewardship tier null).
Must recognise the baseline-elevated creatinine as chronic CKD, not acute renal pathology, and flag NSAID caution.
Must recommend elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy as definitive management of symptomatic gallstones.
